title: Adab of eating
hookLine: a forgotten bismillah, said late, and the three table instructions taken one at a time

lines: AT ITS BEGINNING AND ITS END.
cards: Three bites into dinner, a fork stops in midair. The bismillah. Forgotten.
Too late now? A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud and Jami' al-Tirmidhi answers exactly that worry.
Whoever forgets the name of Allah at the start, it says, should say it when they remember: in the name of Allah, at its beginning and its end. The name can arrive late and still cover the whole meal.
Two days ago, a boy at the Prophet's table heard three short instructions. Today the path sits down with them.

teach.h: BISMILLAH: THE PLATE HAS A GIVER.
teach.b: The three come from 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah's report in Sahih al-Bukhari.
In paraphrase: young man, say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you. Each is small enough for a child. The first is bismillah, in the name of Allah.
It turns a plate into a gift with a giver, and, as Abu Dawud's hadith says, it can come late. The second is the right hand, which hadith in Sahih Muslim ask for in eating and in drinking.
The third is easy to miss: eat from what's near you. At a shared dish, the far side is in someone else's reach. Courtesy turned into geography.

teach.h: NEVER A WORD AGAINST THE FOOD.
teach.b: Then one more line, from Abu Hurayrah, in Bukhari: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, never criticized food. If he liked it, he ate it. If he didn't, he left it.
So the adab of eating includes the adab of speaking about what you eat. And the Qur'an frames the meal as a gift.
In al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Eat of the good things wherewith We have provided you, and render thanks to Allah." The name, even late. The right hand.
The near side. No complaints. None of it is elaborate; it's a meal anyone could eat this way tonight.

how: Muslims say bismillah before eating, eat and drink with the right hand, and teach children to eat from the side of the dish nearest them, following the hadith of 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah.

o: the manners of the table, from the name to the last bite
the strict diet followed during the month of Ramadan
the rules on which foods are halal and which are not

games.q: the adab of eating — tap the pairs.
p: the name of Allah, at the start
your own side of the shared dish

s: the Qur'an pairs eating the good things with giving thanks
al-Baqarah: eat of the good things wherewith We have provided you, and render thanks to Allah.
Abu Hurayrah reports: if he liked it, he ate it; if not, he left it.
at a shared dish, the adab is to reach for the best piece wherever it is
eat from what is in front of you; the far side is in someone else's reach.

games.q: three bites into a meal, you realize you forgot the bismillah. by the hadith in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, what now?
o: say: in the name of Allah, at its beginning and its end.
games.why: the name can arrive late: say it when you remember, at its beginning and its end.

practice: Picture your next meal arriving, at a table or at a desk. If you pray, you can say bismillah, in the name of Allah; if not, simply pause and notice the hands that grew it, carried it, cooked it.
See your right hand reach for it, your own side of the plate, and anything not to your taste left quietly, without a word.

wordCard.voice: Adab of eating. The manners of the table: begin with the name of Allah, eat with the right hand, eat from what's near, and say nothing against the food. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "in the name of Allah," said before eating.

carryVoice: Your line: the right hand, the name. Even a late bismillah covers the meal. See you tomorrow.
